paragraphs: Public health programs must allocate limited resources while their priorities change. Restless multi-armed bandit models have helped with allocation across large populations, but adapting their policies to new preferences can be difficult. This paper introduces a Decision Language Model, or DLM, that lets people express desired policy changes in ordinary language.

The system uses a language model to interpret those preferences and propose reward functions as executable code. Those rewards specify what the allocation system should favor. It then evaluates the proposed functions through RMAB simulations and uses the resulting feedback to revise them. This connects a human request to a concrete decision objective, with simulated consequences informing the next revision.

The authors illustrate the approach through a collaboration with ARMMAN, which allocates health worker calls to underserved populations of pregnant mothers. Their technology demonstration uses Gemini Pro in simulation and shows that human prompts can dynamically shape policy outcomes. The stated result concerns simulated policy adaptation; it does not establish improvements in deployed health outcomes.
neurips-2024-a-decision-language-model-d.tldr: DLM translates public health policy preferences into reward functions and refines them through simulations to adapt resource allocation.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can recognize categories without task-specific examples yet still struggle when test images differ from its training data. CLIPCEIL addresses this domain generalization problem by adapting CLIP to emphasize information that identifies classes across domains. The target test datasets are unavailable during this adaptation.

Its first component is a lightweight adapter that refines visual feature channels. Training reduces variation between domains while increasing variation between classes, encouraging features that remain useful despite changes in the data source. A second component aligns image representations with text descriptions of their classes while further suppressing domain-specific information. These objectives connect visual robustness with the class meaning provided by language.

CLIPCEIL also combines CLIP features at multiple scales through a self-attention module implemented as one Transformer layer. The authors report better performance than existing state-of-the-art methods across five benchmark datasets. These results support the combined strategy of refining visual channels, preserving image-text correspondence, and integrating multiple feature scales for the evaluated distribution shifts.
neurips-2024-clipceil-domain-generalizat.tldr: CLIPCEIL improves domain generalization by refining CLIP’s visual channels, aligning images with class descriptions, and combining features across scales.

paragraphs: This paper asks which training images most influenced a particular image produced by a text-to-image model. It defines influence through a demanding test: removing influential images and retraining from scratch would prevent the model from reproducing that output. Searching directly with repeated retraining is computationally impractical, so the authors seek an efficient way to approximate this investigation.

Their method starts from the generated image and simulates unlearning it. They increase the model’s training loss on that image while avoiding catastrophic forgetting of unrelated concepts. They then examine how the losses of training images change after this intervention. Images whose losses shift substantially are identified as influential, using the model’s response to targeted forgetting as an attribution signal.

The authors evaluate this method against retraining from scratch, which they treat as the expensive reference standard for attribution. They report advantages over previous methods. The contribution is an efficiently obtainable influence signal evaluated against the removal-and-retraining definition, connecting a practical attribution procedure to the behavior it is intended to explain.
neurips-2024-data-attribution-for-text-t.tldr: Targeted unlearning of a generated image helps identify influential training images without repeatedly retraining the entire model.

paragraphs: Controlling a complex physical system requires choosing actions whose effects unfold over time while respecting the system’s dynamics. DiffPhyCon approaches this as a generative planning problem. It jointly optimizes the complete control sequence and the physical trajectory, combining a learned generative energy function with predefined control objectives.

This joint formulation lets the method explore entire candidate evolutions and seek near-optimal control sequences. The authors also introduce prior reweighting, which enables the search to find controls that differ substantially from those represented in the training distribution. That matters because useful control behavior may require moving beyond the examples used to learn the generative model.

The evaluation covers a one-dimensional Burgers’ equation task, two-dimensional jellyfish movement, and high-dimensional two-dimensional smoke control. The authors report better performance than the classical, deep learning, and reinforcement learning methods they compare against. For jellyfish, the method discovers a fast-closing, slow-opening pattern consistent with established fluid dynamics findings. They also release the generated jellyfish dataset as a benchmark for further physical control research.
neurips-2024-diffphycon-a-generative-app.tldr: DiffPhyCon jointly generates physical trajectories and control sequences, using prior reweighting to discover effective controls beyond the training distribution.

paragraphs: Text-video retrieval often places descriptions and videos in a shared representation space, where matching pairs should be close together. However, the differences between language and video can persist within that space. DITS addresses this remaining modality gap through a diffusion-inspired process that progressively aligns their representations.

The method changes both where this process starts and how it is trained. Instead of starting from a randomly sampled Gaussian point, it begins at the fixed text representation and follows a truncated flow toward the video representation. This uses the existing proximity between the modalities to make the transformation more controllable. It also replaces an L2 objective with contrastive learning, which considers matching and nonmatching pairs together and better reflects retrieval’s ranking task.

Experiments on five benchmark datasets suggest state-of-the-art retrieval performance. The authors also observe improvements in the structure of CLIP’s embedding space. Together, these findings support adapting diffusion ideas to the geometry and ranking requirements of retrieval, with the text representation providing a stable starting point for progressive alignment.
neurips-2024-diffusion-inspired-truncate.tldr: DITS improves text-video retrieval through a controlled alignment process that starts from text embeddings and learns with contrastive loss.

paragraphs: An activation function shapes how a neural network transforms information as it passes through the model. This paper argues for making that transformation responsive to graph data in graph neural networks. Its proposed function, DiGRAF, learns a flexible activation that adapts to the graph instead of relying on a fixed transformation.

DiGRAF builds on Continuous Piecewise-Affine Based transformations and adds another graph neural network to learn the adaptive function. The resulting transformation is diffeomorphic: its shape can change while retaining a smooth, invertible structure. The activation and the surrounding model are learned together through end-to-end training, making adaptation part of the network’s learning process.

The authors emphasize that flexibility comes with other useful properties, including differentiability, boundedness within the domain, and computational efficiency. Across experiments spanning diverse datasets and tasks, DiGRAF consistently outperforms the traditional and graph-specific activation functions used for comparison. These findings suggest that the activation itself is a productive place to incorporate graph-dependent behavior, alongside the other learned components of a GNN.
neurips-2024-digraf-diffeomorphic-graph-.tldr: DiGRAF learns smooth, graph-adaptive activation functions and reports consistent improvements over the activation functions evaluated.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization, or SAM, can improve generalization, but the reasons for its effectiveness remain incompletely understood. This paper studies its training dynamics using the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian as a measure of sharpness. That quantity captures the strongest local curvature of the training loss.

The authors develop a third-order stochastic differential equation describing SAM’s dynamics. Their analysis reveals a mixture of second- and third-order effects and highlights the direction of SAM’s perturbation. Effective sharpness regularization depends crucially on alignment between that perturbation and the Hessian’s leading eigenvector, the direction associated with its largest eigenvalue. They find that this alignment is often inadequate in practice, limiting SAM’s efficiency.

These insights motivate Eigen-SAM, which explicitly aligns the perturbation with the leading eigenvector to target the largest eigenvalue. The authors report comprehensive experiments supporting both their theoretical account and the practical benefits of the algorithm. The contribution connects an explanation of when SAM’s perturbations are effective with a concrete change intended to make that alignment more reliable.
neurips-2024-explicit-eigenvalue-regular.tldr: Eigen-SAM targets loss sharpness by aligning SAM’s perturbation with the leading Hessian eigenvector, addressing a weakness identified in its training dynamics.

paragraphs: Algorithms with predictions aim to benefit from accurate forecasts while retaining useful guarantees when forecasts are wrong. This paper examines a fairness problem in a prediction-assisted secretary algorithm. Even with a strong guarantee on the expected value of the selected candidate, the existing algorithm can give the best candidate no chance of selection.

The authors treat that exclusion as unfair and design an algorithm that preserves the value guarantee while ensuring a constant positive probability of selecting the best candidate. The retained guarantee combines a constant-factor fallback with performance approaching the optimum as prediction error decreases. Thus, protection against poor predictions and access for the best candidate are established together.

The algorithm uses a new idea called pegging, which also simplifies or unifies some earlier results. The authors extend their approach to the setting where multiple candidates may be selected and supplement the theory with experiments. The key distinction is between high expected selection value and a meaningful selection chance for the best individual; the paper shows how to guarantee both in its setting.
neurips-2024-fair-secretaries-with-unfai.tldr: A new secretary algorithm preserves prediction-assisted value guarantees while giving the best candidate a constant positive chance of selection.

paragraphs: High-level visual representations capture abstract concepts but lose precise spatial detail, while lower-level representations retain location and simpler features. This paper investigates how abstract context can guide those local sensory responses. It introduces DCnet, a trainable model of visual pathway dynamics designed around biologically motivated connections and neuron types.

DCnet includes local, lateral, and feedforward connections, excitatory and inhibitory neurons, and long-range top-down inputs. These top-down signals act as low-rank modulations of sensory responses. In a cue-delay-search task, the network uses its own representation of the cue to adapt its subsequent perceptual processing. The authors report that it outperforms the state-of-the-art vision and language models evaluated on that task.

The evolution of the model’s population activity provides an account of contextual modulation and generates predictions for experiments. After fine-tuning on classic attention tasks, the same model closely reproduces known reaction time findings. These results position DCnet as a promising tool for investigating context-dependent vision and predicting the effects of perturbations to visual processing.
neurips-2024-flexible-context-driven-sen.tldr: DCnet models how high-level context dynamically modulates sensory processing, with strong task performance and close matches to known attention reaction times.

paragraphs: Flow-based image generators learn a velocity field that guides samples along a generation trajectory. Although their trajectories can be relatively straight, efficient sampling has received less attention than in diffusion models. FlowTurbo accelerates this process using the observation that velocity predictions become stable during sampling.

That stability allows a lightweight velocity refiner to estimate the velocity. The framework also introduces a pseudo corrector and sample-aware compilation to reduce inference time further. It retains multi-step sampling, allowing it to support uses such as image editing and inpainting. Its design therefore speeds up the existing generation process while preserving a sampling structure useful across tasks.

Across the evaluated models, the authors report acceleration ratios of 53.1–58.3% for class-conditional generation and 29.8–38.5% for text-to-image generation. On ImageNet, they report FID values of 2.12 at 100 milliseconds per image and 3.93 at 38 milliseconds per image. These measurements demonstrate the reported speed-quality operating points, supporting the paper’s claim of real-time generation and improved sampling quality in its evaluations.
neurips-2024-flowturbo-towards-real-time.tldr: FlowTurbo accelerates flow-based image generation with a lightweight velocity refiner and additional sampling optimizations while improving reported sampling quality.

paragraphs: A graph encoder pretrained on one dataset can be difficult to reuse when another dataset represents its nodes with differently shaped features. Rebuilding the model sacrifices direct transfer, while forcing features into a common shape can discard information. FUG addresses this compatibility problem through a feature-universal contrastive pretraining strategy.

The authors first establish that PCA’s optimization objective is a special case of a contrastive learning objective. They use this connection to design an encoder that learns to produce basis transformation matrices under contrastive constraints. These matrices adapt features across datasets in a way the authors describe as lossless, avoiding the model rebuilding and feature reshaping required by the alternatives discussed.

FUG also replaces negative sampling with a global uniformity constraint, reducing the stated time complexity from quadratic to linear in n. Explicitly defined positive samples avoid the large memory demands of data augmentation. In cross-domain experiments, its performance approaches that of newly retrained models, suggesting that feature compatibility and efficient pretraining can support reuse across graph datasets.
neurips-2024-fug-feature-universal-graph.tldr: FUG transfers graph encoders across different node-feature shapes through learned basis transformations and a more efficient contrastive objective.

paragraphs: Latent diffusion systems depend on an autoencoder that maps images into a compressed representation and reconstructs them. Although image generation has advanced rapidly, this component’s design remains comparatively underexplored. LiteVAE investigates how to make the autoencoder more efficient while preserving the quality needed by latent diffusion models.

Its design incorporates the two-dimensional discrete wavelet transform to improve scalability and computational efficiency. The authors also study training methods and the decoder architecture, introducing changes that improve training dynamics and reconstruction quality. This treats both the representation design and the way it is trained as opportunities to reduce the cost of the autoencoder.

The base LiteVAE matches the quality of established autoencoders used in current latent diffusion systems while using one-sixth as many encoder parameters. The authors connect this reduction to faster training and lower GPU memory requirements. Their larger model also exceeds similarly complex VAEs on every evaluated metric: rFID, LPIPS, PSNR, and SSIM. The results support efficiency gains at the base size and quality gains at comparable larger complexity.
neurips-2024-litevae-lightweight-and-eff.tldr: LiteVAE uses wavelet-based autoencoder design to match established reconstruction quality with six times fewer encoder parameters.

paragraphs: Offline multi-agent learning must derive coordinated behavior from existing datasets without collecting further interactions. Diffusion models offer an expressive way to model behavior, but applying them separately to each agent can undermine coordination. Combining all agents’ information by simple concatenation can also lead to poor sample efficiency.

MADiff addresses these issues with an attention-based diffusion model that represents relationships among agents’ behaviors. Its framework supports both decentralized policies and a centralized controller. During decentralized execution, it also models teammates, allowing the representation of other agents’ behavior to accompany individual decision-making. In its centralized form, the model can additionally predict multi-agent trajectories.

The authors report that MADiff outperforms baseline algorithms across several multi-agent learning tasks. They present it, to their knowledge, as the first diffusion-based framework for multi-agent learning. The findings support attention-based diffusion as a way to capture complex coordination within offline data, while the two execution modes show how that shared modeling approach can serve different forms of multi-agent control.
neurips-2024-madiff-offline-multi-agent-.tldr: MADiff uses attention-based diffusion to learn coordinated multi-agent behavior from offline data for decentralized and centralized execution.

paragraphs: Computing Jacobians is a recurring cost in fields ranging from machine learning to fluid dynamics. Small computational savings can therefore matter when these calculations are repeated extensively. This paper uses reinforcement learning to reduce the multiplication count required for automatic differentiation while retaining the exact Jacobian.

The method builds on cross-country elimination, which expresses Jacobian accumulation as a sequence of vertex eliminations on a computational graph. Each elimination has a cost, and the order determines the total number of multiplications. The authors frame the search for a low-cost ordering as a single-player game played by a reinforcement learning agent. The learned decision is how to organize the derivative computation.

Across several relevant tasks, the authors report improvements of up to 33% over state-of-the-art methods. They also implement a cross-country elimination interpreter in JAX that executes the discovered orders and demonstrates actual runtime gains. This connects savings in the arithmetic formulation to executable performance, showing that optimizing the order of exact computation can deliver practical benefits.
neurips-2024-optimizing-automatic-differ.tldr: A reinforcement learning agent finds cheaper elimination orders for exact Jacobian computation, with reported arithmetic and runtime improvements.

paragraphs: Discovering causal relationships from observations generally requires assumptions about the relationships or their noise. Many existing methods focus on settings assumed to contain entirely linear or entirely nonlinear relationships. CaPS addresses datasets containing a mixture, making that combination central to the causal discovery procedure.

The algorithm first uses a new criterion to identify a topological ordering, an ordering compatible with the directions of the proposed causal relationships. During post-processing, it introduces parent scores that quantify the strength of average causal effects. These scores guide pruning, helping the algorithm remove proposed relationships more quickly and correct inaccurate predictions made during that step.

On synthetic datasets with different proportions of linear and nonlinear relationships, the proposed solutions outperform the state-of-the-art baselines evaluated. Results on real-world data also support CaPS’s competitiveness. The contribution combines an ordering criterion with effect-based guidance for refining the resulting graph. Its findings support handling mixed relationship types within one discovery approach, while the abstract retains the general need for assumptions when inferring causality from observations.
neurips-2024-ordering-based-causal-disco.tldr: CaPS combines a causal ordering criterion with parent scores to discover and refine mixed linear and nonlinear causal relationships.

paragraphs: Efficiently computing equilibria becomes challenging when a game has a compact description but an enormous underlying strategy space. A known algorithm, Ellipsoid Against Hope, handles correlated equilibria in many compactly represented games, yet does not directly cover sequential games. This paper generalizes that algorithmic machinery to reach a broader family of equilibrium problems.

The authors develop a framework for finding saddle points in bilinear zero-sum games even when one dimension is exponentially large. It requires a good-enough-response oracle, a weaker requirement than an oracle that always supplies a best response. They use this machinery to compute exact linear Phi-equilibria in polyhedral games under the stated mild assumptions.

The framework includes familiar correlated equilibrium notions for both normal-form and extensive-form games. It also yields the first polynomial-time algorithm for exact linear-deviation correlated equilibria in extensive-form games, resolving the identified open question. For cases already known to be tractable, the authors offer a conceptually simpler route. The results concern exact computation within the framework’s assumptions, including its oracle requirements.
neurips-2024-polynomial-time-computation.tldr: A generalized equilibrium-computation framework gives polynomial-time algorithms for exact linear Phi-equilibria under mild assumptions.

paragraphs: Robot learning still struggles to generalize learned behavior to new tasks. This paper investigates the hypothesis that reusable low-level skills can emerge by compressing action sequences into a latent representation. Such temporal abstractions represent behavior extending across time, providing a possible basis for transferring skills between tasks.

The proposed Quantized Skill Transformer, or QueST, learns a larger and more flexible latent encoding than the architectures discussed in prior work. That extra capacity is intended to represent a broader range of low-level skills. QueST also introduces a causal inductive bias from action sequences into the latent space, shaping the representation so that its flexibility produces more meaningful and transferable skill abstractions.

The authors compare QueST with state-of-the-art imitation learning and latent variable model baselines on multitask and few-shot learning benchmarks. They report strong performance across several benchmarks. These findings support the architecture as a promising direction for reusable skills, with its contribution centered on the combination of representational flexibility and structure drawn from action sequences.
neurips-2024-quest-self-supervised-skill.tldr: QueST learns flexible, temporally structured skill representations that show strong results on multitask and few-shot control benchmarks.

paragraphs: Reference-based scene stylization changes a scene’s appearance to match a content-aligned reference image. Existing approaches based on neural radiance fields can produce effective edits, but their volume rendering is costly. ReGS instead adapts a pretrained 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to support real-time viewing of stylized scenes.

The challenge is that discrete Gaussians tie appearance closely to geometry. Changing appearance alone can be insufficient to reproduce the continuous textures in a reference image. ReGS introduces texture-guided control that rearranges the local Gaussians responsible for particular details. Texture cues guide these adjustments, while scene depth provides regularization intended to preserve the original geometric structure.

This combination allows the method to adapt the representation’s arrangement where texture requires it while maintaining guidance from the underlying scene. The authors report state-of-the-art stylization results that respect reference textures and retain real-time rendering for free-view navigation. The contribution is therefore both an editing mechanism suited to Gaussian representations and a way to combine detailed stylization with interactive viewing.
neurips-2024-regs-reference-based-contro.tldr: ReGS rearranges local 3D Gaussians under texture and depth guidance to reproduce reference styles with real-time view synthesis.

paragraphs: Detecting graph nodes that differ from the training distribution requires accounting for connections between nodes. Detection methods developed for other data types may overlook that structure. This paper studies score propagation, a simple procedure that passes out-of-distribution scores among neighboring nodes after the original scores have been computed.

Because propagation operates on scores, it can be combined with existing scoring functions. However, using neighboring information is not automatically beneficial. The authors derive conditions under which propagation helps, providing a theoretical basis for understanding its effectiveness. This moves the analysis beyond observing that a convenient post-processing operation often works.

Those conditions motivate an edge augmentation strategy with a theoretical guarantee. The strategy changes the graph connections used by the method in light of the analysis. Empirical evaluations show improvements over strong out-of-distribution detection baselines across various settings. The central contribution is the connection between a flexible existing operation, a characterization of when it is beneficial, and a graph modification strategy informed by that characterization.
neurips-2024-revisiting-score-propagatio.tldr: The paper derives when graph-based OOD score propagation helps and uses those conditions to design a theoretically supported edge augmentation strategy.

paragraphs: Watermarks in generated images need to remain detectable after modification while avoiding visible artifacts. Weakening a watermark can conceal it, but can also make it less robust. ROBIN addresses this tradeoff by introducing an explicit hiding process that allows stronger watermarks to be embedded.

The method inserts a robust watermark into an intermediate state of diffusion generation. It then guides the remaining generation process to conceal that watermark in the finished image. An adversarial optimization procedure adjusts a prompt embedding to reduce visible artifacts while optimizing the watermark for strength. Each watermark receives its own optimized hiding signal, coupling robustness and concealment within the generation process.

Verification reverses the generation process to check for the watermark. In experiments across multiple diffusion models, the authors find that watermarks remain verifiable after substantial image tampering and are less visible than those from the state-of-the-art robust watermarking methods compared. These results support actively optimizing concealment as a way to improve the robustness-visibility tradeoff in the tested settings.
neurips-2024-robin-robust-and-invisible-.tldr: ROBIN embeds strong diffusion watermarks and optimizes a hiding signal to preserve verifiability while reducing visible artifacts.

paragraphs: Dense linear layers consume much of the computation in large neural networks. This paper searches for structured alternatives while asking how well they perform when model size and the number of training examples are jointly allocated for a given compute budget. That perspective evaluates the full training tradeoff.

The authors introduce a unified search framework covering linear operators expressible through Einstein summation. It includes established structures such as low-rank, Kronecker, Tensor-Train, and Monarch operators, as well as new possibilities. A taxonomy based on computational and algebraic properties provides insight into scaling behavior. Combined with empirical evaluation, it identifies structures that match or exceed dense-layer performance as a function of training compute.

The authors then extend successful structures into a sparse mixture-of-experts layer to improve compute efficiency further. For GPT-2 language models, the resulting layer significantly outperforms dense layers in compute-optimal training efficiency. The contribution connects a broad, systematic space of layer designs to an empirical evaluation of how efficiently those designs turn training computation into model performance.
neurips-2024-searching-for-efficient-lin.tldr: A unified search over structured linear operators identifies compute-efficient layers and a sparse expert extension that improves GPT-2 training efficiency.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization depends on how quickly workers compute updates and communicate them to a central server. Shadowheart SGD studies a setting where communication takes meaningful time and each worker may have different computation and communication speeds. The optimization problems are stochastic and nonconvex, and the workers operate asynchronously.

The method uses unbiased compression to reduce communication while retaining correctness in expectation for the compressed quantities. Its analysis explicitly includes both worker computation and communication delays. The authors prove improved time complexity over previous centralized methods, addressing elapsed time in a heterogeneous system rather than treating communication as a negligible part of optimization.

They also prove that Shadowheart SGD’s time complexity is optimal within the family of centralized methods using compressed communication. That family defines the scope of the optimality claim. Finally, they examine bidirectional communication, where the server’s broadcasts to workers also incur substantial delays, and develop a corresponding method. The paper therefore covers both costly worker-to-server updates and a broader setting with costly communication in both directions.
neurips-2024-shadowheart-sgd-distributed.tldr: Shadowheart SGD achieves provably optimal time complexity within centralized methods with compressed communication under heterogeneous worker speeds and communication delays.

paragraphs: Feature attribution and data valuation can require expensive calculations for every example. This makes otherwise useful explanation methods difficult to apply to large datasets. Amortization offers a way to share that computational work: train a model to predict the desired attribution or valuation output directly.

The difficulty is obtaining accurate targets for training such a model. Computing enough exact labels may recreate the same expense that amortization is meant to avoid. This paper instead investigates training with noisy labels that are inexpensive to obtain. The authors analyze the label noise theoretically and test the approach across different models and datasets, finding that substantial noise can be tolerated.

The resulting approach accelerates several feature attribution and data valuation methods, often by an order of magnitude compared with existing approaches. These findings suggest that exact training targets are not always needed for useful amortized explanations. The contribution is a common strategy for reducing repeated explanation costs by learning from approximate targets, supported by both noise analysis and empirical evaluation.
neurips-2024-stochastic-amortization-a-u.tldr: Training attribution predictors with inexpensive noisy labels tolerates substantial noise and often speeds up explanation methods by an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Testable learning replaces hard-to-verify distribution assumptions with a test that can be checked efficiently. The tester must accept data satisfying the original assumptions, and learning must succeed whenever it accepts. This paper studies testers that must accept standard Gaussian data, focusing on polynomial threshold functions of arbitrary constant degree.

The authors show that these functions can be learned testably to excess error epsilon in time n raised to a polynomial in 1/epsilon. This qualitatively matches the best known guarantees in the distribution-specific agnostic setting. The result extends the reach of testable learning beyond simpler classes such as halfspaces without introducing a qualitatively worse runtime guarantee.

The proof uses a connection to fooling: distributions that approximately match sufficiently many Gaussian moments behave similarly to the Gaussian when evaluated by constant-degree polynomial threshold functions. The required moment count is polynomial in 1/epsilon. The authors also establish that a direct proof approach previously successful for halfspaces cannot work for these functions, clarifying why their alternative route through fooling is useful.
neurips-2024-testably-learning-polynomia.tldr: Constant-degree polynomial threshold functions admit testable learning guarantees that qualitatively match known agnostic learning runtimes.

paragraphs: Conformal prediction produces sets intended to contain the true output with a user-chosen probability. Its standard coverage guarantee relies on exchangeability of training and test data. Adversarial perturbations can undermine that guarantee, motivating methods that account explicitly for how attacks affect predictions.

VRCP uses neural network verification methods to recover coverage guarantees under adversarial attacks. Earlier approaches described in the paper rely on randomized smoothing and support classification with L2-bounded perturbations. VRCP extends support to regression and perturbations bounded by arbitrary norms, including L1, L2, and L-infinity. This broadens both the kinds of output that can receive protection and the ways an allowed attack can be bounded.

The authors evaluate image classification on CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet, together with regression tasks from deep reinforcement learning environments. In every evaluated case, coverage exceeds the nominal target, and the prediction regions are more efficient and informative than those of the state-of-the-art methods compared. The empirical results complement the framework’s guarantees by showing useful prediction regions in the tested attack settings.
neurips-2024-verifiably-robust-conformal.tldr: VRCP uses neural network verification to provide adversarially robust conformal prediction for classification and regression under arbitrary norm-bounded perturbations.
